# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review of "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay"

The arithmetic in the paper checks out:
- Sector counts sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees.
- The employee-weighted output index is 98.73.
- Each "output per scheduled hour" figure equals the sector's index divided by 0.8.
- The sick-day (−36.4%) and resignation (−56.3%) changes are correct.

The problems are interpretive. Several of the headline claims are either mechanical consequences of the design or contradicted by the paper's own data.

## 1. The "gain in every sector" is guaranteed by the arithmetic

Output per scheduled hour is the output index divided by 0.8. So any sector whose output fell by *less than 20%* will show a gain. A sector whose output fell 15% would report "+6% productivity per hour."

That makes "every sector shows a substantial increase" and "consistency across sectors" non-findings. They would be true almost regardless of what happened. The informative quantity is the output index itself, and on that measure:
- Output fell in five of six sectors.
- Only software and IT exceeded 100. Professional services was essentially flat at 99.8.
- The pilot's own stated principle, "100% of the output," was not met overall (98.7) or in most sectors.
- Retail and hospitality lost 6.9% of output at unchanged pay. That is roughly a 7.4% rise in labour cost per unit of output (100/93.1).

Recommendation: lead with the output index and unit labour cost. Present output per scheduled hour as a derived figure, with an explicit note that it is mechanically positive whenever output falls by less than 20%.

## 2. The paper's own data contradict "sector-general"

The Discussion cites retail and hospitality as the strongest evidence for generality. The Continuation section says the opposite:

| Sector | Organisations | Reverted | Reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Office sectors (prof. services, IT, marketing, non-profit) | 50 | 0 | 0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 2 | 40% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | **50%** |

Half the retail and hospitality organisations reverted, and that sector had the largest output loss. The evidence actually supports a much narrower conclusion: the model held up well in office and knowledge work, and much less well in customer-facing and coverage-bound work. Six retail organisations and five healthcare administration organisations are also too few to support sector-level claims in either direction.

## 3. Selection and attrition

- **Withdrawals.** Nine of 70 enrolled organisations (13%) withdrew during preparation, "chiefly for scheduling reasons." Scheduling difficulty is exactly the failure mode you would expect from coverage-bound organisations. These dropouts should be reported by sector. Ideally, results should also be shown on an intention-to-treat basis.
- **Overall persistence.** Counting withdrawals (9) and reversions (5), 14 of 70 organisations (20%) did not sustain the model. That is a more honest denominator than 56 of 61.
- **Meaning of "continue."** Only 18 organisations made the change permanent. The other 38 "continued," which may mean an extended trial. The 92% figure should be split accordingly.

## 4. Measurement problems the Limitations section underweights

**Output index.** It is self-reported by the managers responsible for the pilot, and it is built from heterogeneous records with no common definition. The headline result (98.7 versus 100) is a 1.3-point difference. A manager-reporting bias of a few points, which is entirely plausible, is the same size as the effect being claimed. "Unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size" does not hold, because the large size is the mechanical ratio from issue 1, not the output change.

**Seasonality is handled inconsistently.**
- Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year, specifically to remove seasonality.
- Output and sick days are compared with the *preceding* six months, which keeps seasonality in.

If the baseline covered winter and the pilot covered spring and summer, sick days would fall for that reason alone. Output could shift in either direction depending on the business.

**Sick days per year fall mechanically with a four-day week.** Staff have 20% fewer scheduled days on which to take sick leave. At unchanged per-day sickness rates, 4.4 days per year would become about 3.5. The observed 2.8 is roughly a 20% reduction per scheduled day, not 36%. Report sick days per scheduled day.

**Revenue is nominal and incomplete.**
- It is +1.4% nominal. If the pilot ran in 2023, inflation in most economies was well above 1.4%, which would make this a real-terms decline.
- Nine organisations did not report revenue. Their sectors should be stated.

**Hours.** Only scheduled hours are reported. If staff worked on days off or lengthened their remaining days, the true reduction in hours is smaller. Separately, organisations using staggered days (17) may have kept coverage through overtime or extra hiring. The paper reports no headcount or staffing-cost data. That omission matters most in exactly the sectors that struggled.

**Resignations.** Annualised from six months of data, this is roughly 46 resignations against about 104 expected. Two alternative explanations need addressing:
- Employees have a strong incentive to stay *while a perk is on offer*.
- Labour-market conditions may have changed during the pilot, and there is no control group to separate that out.

**Survey.**
- Response rates are not reported.
- "71% reported lower burnout than at baseline" is a retrospective judgement, which is prone to bias.
- "Rating own productivity higher than before" has no baseline, so it cannot show change.

## 5. The mechanism claim is not supported, and partly contradicted

The Discussion calls reduced fatigue "the most plausible single explanation." But:
- **Energy fades.** It rose 0.61 SD at month three, then dropped to 0.29 SD at month six, roughly halving. That pattern fits a novelty or Hawthorne effect at least as well as sustained rest. It also makes the six-month duration limitation more serious, not less.
- **Process changes are a strong rival explanation.** The interviews describe fewer meetings, focus blocks and less reporting, and managers called the schedule "a forcing device" for changes they had long wanted. Those process changes could plausibly explain whatever output was maintained, and many of them could be adopted without cutting hours.
- **The design can't separate the two.** With no control group and no measurement of each change's contribution, it cannot distinguish fatigue, process change, selection, or reporting bias.

## 6. Continuation is weak evidence of output

Reverting is visibly costly to morale and retention, and these organisations self-selected because they were enthusiastic. A high continuation rate shows that participating organisations found the model acceptable. It does not independently corroborate output. In any case, the reversion pattern (issue 2) points against generality.

## Summary of where the claims stand

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Output near-maintained overall | Plausible, but rests on a manager-reported measure whose likely bias is the same size as the effect |
| +23.4% output per hour | Arithmetic restatement of "output fell 1.3%"; not independent evidence |
| Gains in every sector | Mechanically guaranteed; uninformative |
| Sector-general model | Contradicted by retail output (−6.9%) and reversions (50% retail, 40% healthcare administration) |
| Sick days −36% | About −20% after adjusting for fewer working days; seasonality uncontrolled |
| Revenue shows no sacrifice | Nominal, with 9 organisations missing; possibly a real decline |
| Fatigue is the mechanism | Untested; energy decay and process changes offer competing explanations |
| 92% continuation | 18 permanent; 20% of enrolees did not sustain the model |

## Suggested revisions

1. Make the output index and unit labour cost the headline. Present output per scheduled hour with a caveat that it is mechanically positive whenever output falls less than 20%.
2. Rewrite the sector conclusion to something like: "results were strongest in office and knowledge-work sectors; evidence in customer-facing sectors is limited and mixed."
3. Report withdrawals and reversions by sector, and give an intention-to-treat summary.
4. Use a year-earlier baseline for output and sick days, as you already do for revenue. Report sick days per scheduled day. Deflate revenue for inflation.
5. Report actual hours where available, plus headcount and overtime changes, especially for the 17 organisations with staggered days off.
6. Report survey response rates. Present the decay in energy as a finding in its own right.
7. Remove "unlikely to overturn the main result" from the Limitations section, or justify it with sensitivity analyses. For example, how much manager bias would it take to push output to 95, or to 90?

I can redraft the Summary and Discussion along these lines, or sketch the sensitivity analyses, if that would help.
